headline: The DOJ tried to charge a Jan. 6 witness. Jurors said no.
summary: Cassidy Hutchinson told Congress in 2022 that Trump knew some January 6 supporters were armed and grabbed for the wheel of his SUV. Republicans say she lied under oath and asked the DOJ to charge her. On Tuesday a grand jury in Washington refused to indict, two people familiar told AP. It is the DOJ's latest setback in charging Trump's critics.

cover_question.q: Who gets to tell the DOJ no?

cover_answer: Ordinary citizens on a grand jury. Tuesday, they did.
table_question: If you repeat something a friend told you and it's wrong, did you lie?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: A woman named Cassidy Hutchinson once told Congress what she said she saw at the White House. Some people said she made it up and wanted her punished. On Tuesday a group of ordinary people listened and said there's no case, the way a whole class has to agree before anyone gets a time-out. Nobody is hurt, and the grown-ups have it.
5-7.why: She told what she saw, and a group said no case.
5-7.why_long: A six-year-old reads your face before the words, and this story has a crowd and a president in it they don't need. So the card keeps one thing: a woman told what she saw, and when some people wanted her punished, a group of ordinary people said no. Expect "did she tell the truth?" Nobody has proved she didn't.

8-12.script: Cassidy Hutchinson, a Trump aide, told Congress in 2022 that Trump knew some January 6 supporters were armed and grabbed for the wheel of his SUV. Republicans wanted her charged with lying. A grand jury of citizens checks the evidence first. Tuesday's said no, like a referee waving off a penalty.
8-12.why: Citizens check the evidence first. The referee is the mechanism.
8-12.why_long: This age is testing whether adults apply the rules evenly, so the script hands them the check that comes before a charge: a grand jury of citizens, and this one said no. The referee waving off the penalty is the mechanism. Expect "so was she lying?" Not proven. The driver denied the grab and backed the rest.

13-17.script: Is partly wrong testimony a crime? Cassidy Hutchinson told Congress Trump grabbed for his SUV's wheel; the driver denied that but confirmed Trump tried to reach the Capitol. Tuesday a grand jury refused to charge her with lying. Second: it's the DOJ's latest failed case against a critic. Why?
13-17.why: Secondhand and partly wrong is not a lie. Let them draw the line.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things at once: her wheel story was secondhand and the driver denied it, and the same driver backed her on Trump trying to reach the Capitol. The script asks where testimony becomes a crime and lets them draw the line first. Expect "will they try again?" I don't know. The reports don't say.

5-7.a: No. The people who decide said there wasn't a case, so there's no charge.

8-12.q: Who gets to tell the DOJ no?
8-12.a: Citizens who hear the evidence before a charge. Tuesday's said no.
Not proven. The driver denied the grab but backed the rest.

13-17.a: Not proven. The driver denied the grab and backed the rest.

13-17.q: Is this the DOJ going after Trump's enemies?
13-17.a: AP calls it the DOJ's latest setback charging Trump's perceived foes.
